title: The Count Ends at Two
passages:
Wind came up the dry spillway in one long push, and the trestle plates ticked under them as they cooled. Wren stood where she was, wrists bare, torn palm pressed inside her coat so it wouldn't drip on the deck.

"I'm the lid-hand," she said.

Coombs took his time. He held the slate flat on his hand the way a man carries a plate to somebody else's table, and he smiled at her like she'd done him a favor. "Say it at the mouth end, friend. It's shy."

She leaned down and said it again, into the grille.

The slate woke. A proving slate is a reader with two blank fields and no opinions. It won't take a badge, a description, or a story. It takes a body saying a claim out loud in its own voice, then it goes and finds the record with that voice in it, reads the record back, and whatever it reads back is what happened, as far as any desk from here to the coast is concerned. One field holds one body. Once it sings a name the field is spent, and the only thing that crosses out a spent field is the desk that wrote it.

The slate read.

"Bay Four. Shift Two. Eleven seals short across four down-line runs. One receiving mark, repeated. Lid counter present at close. Two spoken numerals logged in the box throat, twenty-one forty-four, eleven seconds."

Then, in her own voice, from four hundred kilometers and two days back: *Three.*

The wind took it out over the cut.

*Two.*

"Great," Miko said, from beside the tender's tool void. "It does impressions."

"Twenty-one forty-four," Coombs said, warm as a kitchen. "Man in that box logged dead at thirty-six point four, and a hot bunk with your name on it going begging. One field left on this slate. Yours is filled. Hers isn't. Say the word and I'll wipe the count, log you both as runners who came in out of the cold, and no desk ever hears a number out of your mouth again."

Boots on plate. The man from the second rig came up out of the dark with the file tube under his arm, unhurried, a Kettering coat with the desk's stripe on the sleeve.

"Adisa Bale," he said. "Remand. I'm carrying a hold order with your bay number on it and a berth on the coast roster, and I'd like the record confirmed for the tube before the hour." He held the tube out flat, cap toward her, polite as a man offering a light. "Confirm it, or say no. The tube takes either one. It doesn't take quiet."

Rhea moved — half a step, hand coming up. "Wren—"

"It's mine," Wren said.

She looked at the slate, at the empty half of its face, at two little numerals sitting in the record like something left out on a counter. Her palm was hot inside the coat. She thought about a bunk, and a wage, and a count that stopped.

"Ask me a different question," she told Bale.

"I only carry the one," he said, and waited, pleasant, while down the line the coast board began dropping its green lamps out one at a time as the hour came up.

Then the slate's second field lit on its own and said, in a flat little voice, *Next body.*

Coombs turned his head toward the tool void.

Miko did not come out of the tool void.

Coombs bent toward it, patient as a man at a henhouse. "Friend. It's rude to leave a slate hanging."

"I'm cargo," Miko said from inside. "Cargo's got no voice. Weigh me."

"Leave her," Rhea said. "It's not going to sing her."

She was already moving, out along the trestle to the switch post, where a cast yard set hung at chest height on a bracket — a speaker grille, a thumb bar, a copper hardline running the length of the ore line to Anza's board, because radio dies in the cut and copper doesn't. She'd used it twice that week to argue with a dispatcher about ice.

"Rhea." Wren's voice cracked on it. "Don't."

"You said two." Rhea put her thumb on the bar. "I've been wrong about a thing for two days that I can go check, and I hate that more than I hate you people."

"Ma'am," Bale said pleasantly, tube still out flat, "the tube takes a confirm or a no. It doesn't take a theory."

"Then don't listen." She keyed the bar. "Anza relay, Weir switch."

The grille hissed. In her coat pocket a spare cartridge lay against her ribs with its scrubber clock already running down from forty minutes; she had about that long before she had to be pointed at Anza whether this went well or not.

"Anza relay." Teodoro, close to the speaker, the way he got when he'd been sitting with somebody's breathing. "Rhea. Your brother's on mains, he's fine, he's insulting my compressor. Also the plate's up, it's all up, green chain, resupply rolling, nobody's touched a canister at Culvert Nine—"

"Read me the plate. The living line. Out loud, all of it."

A pause, paper or a screen. "Marlowe. Shop crew, badge twenty-four forty-four. Countersigned live seal authority, Ospina. Shop-hand duty assigned, bunk two, shoulder splinted. Status living, breathing, mains power. He's got a cup on my table and he won't let anybody move it." Another pause. "Why do you want—"

"Because there's a man here with a tube." Rhea looked at Wren. "Say the rest of it to her, Teo."

"He's in the next room," Teodoro said. "He's been in the next room since yesterday. He asked twice if the woman was coming back."

The wind went along the trestle plates. Down the line the coast board let go another green lamp.

"A repeater," Rhea said, "is a brick of memory in a pod's neck. It doesn't measure. It holds the last good number the sensors handed it and it says that number in the same flat voice forever, until something new comes up the wire. The databus is the bundle that carries new numbers up the wire. You cut the bundle and you haven't killed the box. You've made a man who keeps giving his answer because nobody ever asked him again."

Wren didn't move.

"Thirty-six point four is a live man's core temperature," Rhea said. "That's the last thing that box heard in Kettering at twenty-one forty-four, with him warm and swearing. Then the loom went, and the box rode four hundred kilometers in the dark repeating it over a body that was freezing, and every desk it talked to wrote down *dead at normal.* Cleanest lie there is. Nobody checks a number that agrees with itself."

Bale's face did something small and unhappy. "That's a story."

"It's a cut loom in a bag on my bench at Anza with your Bay Four crimp on the end of every wire, and I pulled it out with these hands." Rhea held up the hands. "Eleven years I've taken a gauge over a mouth every time. Every time. And the gauge was fed."

Nobody said anything. The slate hummed, one field spent, one field waiting.

Rhea lifted the handset off its hook and held it out across the gap, into Wren's ruined palm. "It's copper all the way to him. Ask him yourself."

Wren reached for the handset and her hand wouldn't do it.

The cut had gone stiff in the cold, tacky at the edges, and the fingers came only halfway around. So she laid the thumb bar down into the meat of the wound and leaned on it, and the copper went slick, and she kept leaning. A yard set is a bar and a grille and a length of wire. Lift the bar and you're a woman talking to herself on a bridge.

"Go ahead," Teodoro said. "I've got you. Take your time. Ivo's asleep and insulting my compressor in his sleep, we're fine here."

Coombs tipped his head, kind as an uncle. "Friend, you don't owe the wire anything. Slate's got you written either way."

"Then stop talking," Wren said.

In Rhea's coat pocket something went on with its arithmetic, small and patient, counting down from forty.

She looked at the grille. The wind came up the spillway and the trestle plates ticked and the coast board let go another green lamp down the line, and she said, "Three."

Her own voice went four hundred kilometers down the copper and did not come back.

She waited. Her palm was burning now, a good clean burn, and she waited long enough that Bale shifted the tube under his arm and Miko said out of the tool void, "Nobody's timing you. Take all night. I've got a bunk in a box."

"Two," Wren said.

Then she stopped with her mouth open, waiting for the next one.

It didn't come. She could feel the shape of the place where it should have been, the way your foot feels for a stair that isn't there. She stood on the trestle with her mouth open in the wind like an idiot, waiting on a number.

A lid-hand holds the crates and counts the seal down loud, so the loader at the stamp knows where the lid is without lifting his eyes. The seal bites at two. Two is where hands come clear. There is no one. There was never a one, not in that bay, not in any bay, not in four years of counting crates shut with her gloves taped at the knuckle because the tape held better than skin. She had carried two numbers four hundred kilometers in the dark and one of them had never been in her mouth at all.

The count ended where it always ended. And it had not been the count that put a man in a box.

"Say the rest of it," Rhea said. Quiet, for her.

Wren leaned harder on the bar. "He was warm," she said. "He was swearing. He said something about his shoulder and then he said a word I'm not saying on an open line, and then the lid came down and I had my hands on it, I was the one holding it, and I counted to two and I never—"

The grille hissed.

Then, from a long way off, from a room with mains power in it, came the sound of a cup being set down on a table. Not dropped. Set down, the way a man does when he wants both hands.

"Hold on," Teodoro said. "Hold on, he's up—"

Boots on a floor. Four hundred kilometers of copper and the boots came through it clear as if the room were the next one over, three steps, four, and something with a splint on it knocking the doorframe on the way.

Wren didn't take her thumb off the bar.

The boots stopped. Something breathed close to the grille, four hundred kilometers away, and then a man's voice said, "Who's got the bar? I want it on the record that I knocked the doorframe, because the operator's going to claim I did it on purpose."

"Marlowe—" Wren said.

"That's the name. Shop crew, bunk two, shoulder splinted, cup going cold." He was low and unhurried and far too awake for a man who'd spent two days as ballast. "You're the dark. Ospina said there was a dark. Nobody told me the dark could talk."

"I counted," Wren said.

"I heard you. Copper carries." A pause, and the sound of him shifting his weight off the bad side. "Three, two. Then you quit, and every soul on that trestle held their breath like the next one was mine to say."

"Ma'am." Bale's voice, pleasant, closer now. "The tube takes a confirm or a no before the hour."

"Don't answer him," Marlowe said. "Answer me."

Rhea's free hand had found her coat pocket and the cartridge in it. She didn't take it out.

"You want to put a zero on me," Marlowe said. "I can hear it in how you're standing. You've got a number in your mouth and you want to spend it on my account, and I'm telling you my account is closed. I'm not down. I'm not ballast. I'm shop crew with my name chalked on the bunk frame and a cup on the operator's table that nobody is allowed to move, and in about ten minutes I'm going to fetch it, because it's mine and it's going cold."

"You were in the dark two days," Wren said.

"So were you. Difference is I had mains power and something to be annoyed about." Something in the room knocked, a chair leg maybe. "I've had nothing on my roster but this. You want to know what you did wrong? You did it bad. That's the whole list. You held that lid like a woman reading out her own sentence and you counted so soft the stamp had to guess at you."

"Then what am I supposed to do with two," Wren said. Her thumb was still on the bar, still leaning.

"Keep it. That's the end of the count and it's the right end. You hear me? A zero needs a body underneath it to hold the weight, and I am standing square in the road of that, shoulder and all. You can't drop a zero on a man who won't lie down and take it." Boots again, one step, like he'd shifted to make the point. "I'm not giving you a one and I'm not giving you a zero. I'm giving you a cup to fetch and a bunk with your name near it, and you can make of that whatever keeps you upright."

Miko's voice came out of the tool void, muffled and interested. "He's better at this than the puller."

"Everybody's better at this than the puller," Coombs said, without heat. He hadn't moved the slate. One field spent, one field waiting, and the waiting one hummed to itself in the wind.

Wren closed her mouth. She stood there with her mouth shut and her palm burning and the shape of the missing stair still under her foot, except now somebody was standing on it, holding it up, complaining about his shoulder.

"Say it back to me," Marlowe said. "The number where you stopped."

"Two."

"Louder. It's an open line and I've got a desk listening."

"Two," she said, and the trestle plates ticked, and the copper took it away down the line and this time it went to a man who was standing.

"Good," Marlowe said. "Now I'm going to get my cup, and the operator's going to fuss, and I'll be right here. Don't you go anywhere, dark."

Boots on a floor, going away, four steps, unhurried. Teodoro, off the grille: "He's not going to sit down. I want that noted by somebody with authority."

Wren lifted her thumb off the bar, half an inch, no more. Behind her the slate sat face-up on Coombs's hand with one field still open, and Bale shifted the sealed tube under his arm and looked at the coast board the way a man looks at a clock he doesn't own.
